questions.title: Inheritance & Interfaces practice 1
questions.prompt: Which declaration lets a class promise the methods in Payable?
choices: class Invoice implements Payable
class Invoice imports Payable
class Invoice includes Payable
class Invoice instanceOf Payable
questions.explanation: The `implements` keyword connects a class to an interface contract. The class must then provide the required abstract methods.

questions.title: Inheritance & Interfaces practice 2

It makes the method private
It permits two return types
It creates the superclass
questions.explanation: The annotation catches misspelled names and mismatched parameters at compile time. It does not change access or create inheritance by itself.

questions.title: Trace Inheritance & Interfaces
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Both classes satisfy Payable, so one list can hold both. The loop calls the version belonging to the actual object. The resulting output is '25.0\n10.0'.

questions.title: Inheritance & Interfaces practice 5
questions.prompt: Why declare the parameter as the interface `Payable` rather than the class `Invoice`?
choices: The method then accepts any type that implements Payable, including future ones
Interfaces run faster than concrete classes
Invoice cannot be printed with println
Only interfaces are allowed as method parameters
questions.explanation: Accepting `Payable` lets the method work with `Invoice`, `Receipt`, or any class that implements the interface, now or later. Requiring `Invoice` locks it to one class. This is about flexibility, not speed, and concrete classes are perfectly valid parameter types too.

questions.title: True is-a relationship
questions.prompt: When is `extends` the right relationship between two Java classes?
choices: Use `extends` for a true is-a relationship. For helper objects, use composition.
Use inheritance only to borrow a helper method.
Extend a class when the child is not really a kind of parent.
Put fields in an interface to share object state.
questions.explanation: `extends` should mean every child object can honestly be used as a parent object. If a class only needs help from another object, composition is clearer and avoids promising an inheritance relationship that is not true.

questions.title: Interface capability
questions.prompt: When should a Java design use an interface?
choices: Depend on concrete classes when a capability contract is enough.
Use an interface to state a capability.
Override a method but change its promised meaning.
Use a superclass to force unrelated classes together.
questions.explanation: An interface names a capability or contract, such as something that can be saved, compared, or displayed. It lets different classes promise the same behavior without forcing them into one parent class.

questions.title: Typing by contract
questions.prompt: Why type a variable as an interface when callers only need that interface's behavior?
choices: Forget that a class can implement more than one interface.
Make callers know every subclass type.
Type variables by the contract when callers need flexibility.
Use inheritance where composition would be simpler.
questions.explanation: Typing by the contract gives callers flexibility. They can work with any implementation that honors the interface, which keeps code from depending on one concrete class too early.

questions.title: Override checking
questions.prompt: Why add `@Override` when a child class replaces a parent or interface method?
choices: Leave abstract behavior undocumented.
Treat an interface as if it stores per-object data.
Break substitutability by narrowing what a child can do.
Use `@Override` for compiler checking.
questions.explanation: `@Override` asks the compiler to verify that a real inherited method is being implemented. It catches misspellings and wrong parameters before the program runs, which is much kinder than a silent non-override.

questions.title: Extends restraint
questions.prompt: A class only wants to reuse a helper method from another class. Why might `extends` be the wrong tool?
choices: Reserve `extends` for a true is-a relationship.
Use casting instead of designing the right contract.
Duplicate shared behavior across subclasses.
Expose parent internals just so a child can work.
questions.explanation: Inheritance makes a public relationship claim, not just a code-sharing shortcut. If the child is not truly a kind of parent, a helper field or separate utility keeps the design honest.

questions.title: Composition for reuse
questions.prompt: When is composition a better choice than a deeper inheritance tree?
choices: Make a deep hierarchy for one small variation.
Prefer composition for simple code reuse.
Ignore method names promised by the interface.
Use `extends` when the relationship is only uses-a.
questions.explanation: Composition lets one object use another object's help without pretending to be that object. It is often simpler for small variations because each class keeps its own identity and delegates only the needed work.
